mcqs.question: What problem does the lakehouse pitch specifically solve, compared to choosing purely between a lake and a warehouse?
options: It eliminates the need for any query engine
It makes object storage unnecessary
It guarantees lower cost than either a lake or a warehouse in every scenario
It removes the forced trade-off between a lake's cost/flexibility and a warehouse's transactional guarantees, by adding those guarantees directly on top of lake storage
mcqs.explanation: The lakehouse pitch is specifically about getting warehouse-grade guarantees on top of cheap, flexible lake storage, avoiding the old either/or choice. It still requires a query engine, still relies on object storage as the underlying substrate, and doesn't guarantee it's cheaper than every alternative in every case.

mcqs.question: A writer crashes halfway through writing new data files for a table update, before the metadata pointer swap happens. What do readers see?
options: The last valid snapshot, unaffected, since the pointer never advanced to reference the incomplete write
A mix of old and new data, since the write was already partially applied
An error, since the table becomes permanently corrupted
The new, incomplete data, since files were already written to storage
mcqs.explanation: Because the pointer swap is the single atomic operation that makes a new version visible, a crash before that swap leaves the pointer unchanged, so readers keep seeing the last complete, valid snapshot — the incomplete files are simply orphaned and never referenced. Nothing here corrupts the table or exposes readers to a partial mix.

mcqs.question: An ML team wants to pin a training run's input data so retraining later uses the exact same data, even if the table has since been updated. What feature solves this?
options: Compaction
Time travel — querying the table as of the specific snapshot used for the original training run
Schema enforcement
Optimistic concurrency control
mcqs.explanation: Time travel lets a query target a specific retained snapshot rather than the current version, which is exactly what pinning a training run's input data requires. Compaction only affects physical file layout, schema enforcement governs structure not historical versions, and concurrency control manages simultaneous writers, not point-in-time reads.

mcqs.question: A source system adds a new column to data being written into a lakehouse table. How does the table format typically handle this without rewriting existing files?
options: It rejects all future writes until every existing file is rewritten with the new column
It deletes the old files and requires re-ingestion of all historical data
It records the schema change in metadata; old files simply lack the column, and readers return null for it on those files
It silently ignores the new column and drops it from all future writes
mcqs.explanation: Schema evolution is handled as a metadata-level change — old files aren't rewritten, and readers are expected to return null for a column that didn't exist when those files were written. Writes aren't rejected, historical files aren't deleted or require re-ingestion, and the new column isn't silently dropped.

mcqs.question: A streaming job commits to a lakehouse table every 30 seconds with no compaction scheduled. What's the resulting query-time cost, and why?
options: No cost, since lakehouse tables automatically compact on every read
Query latency degrades because per-file overhead is roughly fixed, so tens of thousands of tiny accumulated files cost disproportionately more to query than the same data in fewer larger files
The table becomes read-only until manually repaired
Storage cost decreases because small files compress better than large ones
mcqs.explanation: Since per-file overhead (opening, reading metadata, planning) is roughly constant regardless of file size, accumulating tens of thousands of tiny files makes that fixed overhead dominate query time. Tables don't auto-compact on read, they don't become read-only from file count alone, and small-file accumulation doesn't inherently improve compression.

mcqs.question: Two writers attempt to commit updates to the same lakehouse table around the same time. Under optimistic concurrency control, what happens if writer B's pointer-swap attempt occurs after writer A's has already succeeded?
options: The table is locked before either writer starts, preventing this scenario entirely
Both commits are applied and merged automatically into one combined snapshot
Writer B's commit is rejected and it must retry against the newer snapshot writer A created
Writer A's commit is silently rolled back to let writer B proceed
mcqs.explanation: Optimistic concurrency control detects that the snapshot has moved since writer B read it, rejects B's stale commit, and requires B to retry against the current state — it doesn't pre-lock the table, silently merge conflicting writes, or roll back the writer that already succeeded.
